questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [mid] day-2 abuse response on a shared rate limiter (3buildanalytics, docs/upskill/03-architecture-and-patterns/05-pattern-catalog.md). Scenario: the Redis-backed limiter already runs on 4 API instances. A logistics partner's nightly sync legitimately needs about 2,500 requests a minute from one service account, ten times the default budget, and has started seeing refusals. The same week a credential-stuffing run sends roughly 30,000 sign-in attempts an hour from 9,000 residential addresses, never more than 3 from any one address per 15 minutes. Support must be able to tell the partner exactly why and when it was refused. Write your design before you look: how a per-caller allowance fits the existing tier factory and what it is keyed by, how sign-in is protected when no single address trips its limit, how the partner stays out of that blast radius, and what you log and chart about refusals. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] A partner allowance extends the tier model instead of forking it: each tier today is a bucket whose points and window are fixed when the module loads, so the override is a per-account entry (points, window, owner, expiry) looked up on each request, falling back to the static tier and counted under its own bucket prefix so it never mixes with the default counter.

[w3] Do not fix one caller by raising the default: the global budget is a single environment value (250 per 60-second window) applied to every caller, anonymous address-keyed traffic included, so a tenfold raise for the partner is a tenfold raise for every scraper too.

[w2] Look the allowance up by the authenticated account, not by an address allowlist: authentication already runs before the limiter so the account id is known, while an allowlist breaks when the partner rotates its egress and hands the raised budget to anyone sharing that address.

[w3] A run spread over thousands of addresses never trips a per-address limit, so sign-in needs a second key: a failed-attempt budget per target account, keyed by the lower-cased email the login path already normalizes (and already records on every failure).

[w2] Tightening sign-in cannot spend the partner's budget: the credential tier is its own bucket keyed by address even for signed-in callers, while the partner's sync calls data routes with a token, so the two budgets are counted apart and can be tuned independently.

[w2] Make every refusal explainable: the request log already records the request id, route and status, but not which bucket refused or for which caller, so a refusal should log bucket, identifier and the window's reset time, and 429s should be charted per bucket so the partner tier and the sign-in tier are separate lines.
keyPoints.quote: Logs contain method, path, status, duration, requestId.

keyPoints.text: [w2] Failed logins are the stuffing signal: watch the 401 rate and the failed-login tracked events, and alert when failures rise across many addresses and many accounts at once, the shape no single-address limit ever sees.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — a month later: the partner's service-account token is phished and used to scrape at the partner's raised allowance, the stuffing run moves from sign-in to the token-refresh endpoint, an on-call engineer stops a 2 a.m. page about partner refusals by editing the global default, and the stuffing volume is still being written row by row into the analytics tables. What breaks first, and what in your design already handles it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] A raised allowance is a raised budget for whoever holds the credential: scope the override to the routes the sync actually needs, and keep the response to a stolen token fast, since the app can already end every session of one account in a single call.

[w3] Only register and login sit behind the strict credential tier; the refresh, logout and session routes fall back to the global default, so an attacker who moves to refresh gets the generous budget. Every endpoint that accepts a credential needs a deliberate tier.

[w3] Every failed sign-in inserts a tracked-event row, so 30,000 attempts an hour become 30,000 analytics writes that load the database and distort dashboards built on those events; once a run is detected, aggregate or sample the failures instead of storing each one.

[w2] The 2 a.m. edit to the environment default quietly hands every caller on every default-tier route ten times its budget and outlives the incident; the runbook answer to partner refusals is the per-account override, owned and dated.

[w2] Labelling refusal metrics with the caller id creates a time series per user; the collector already records the route pattern rather than the raw URL for exactly this reason, so caller ids belong in the log line and metrics stay per bucket and route.

[w2] A per-account failure budget is also a lever against the victim: anyone who knows an email can keep that account throttled. Prefer slowing to locking, and let the budget lapse with its window, which here happens by key expiry with nothing to reset.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your day-2 choices against the alternatives: a per-account allowance versus raising the global default, a per-account sign-in budget on top of the per-address one versus per-address alone, refusing abuse in the application versus at the edge, recording failed sign-ins as product telemetry versus as security history, keeping caller detail in logs versus in metrics, and who may grant an allowance. For each, say what you bought and what it cost.

keyPoints.text: [w3] A per-account allowance keeps the blast radius to one caller and makes the raise visible as data; it costs a lookup per request and a configuration someone must own and expire, where raising the default costs nothing to ship and weakens every caller at once.

[w3] Adding a per-account budget catches runs spread across many addresses but lets anyone slow a known user's sign-ins; keeping only the per-address limit is fair to victims and blind to spread runs. Running both, with the account budget slowing rather than locking, buys coverage at the price of a second counter per attempt.

[w3] The application limiter knows the user and the route tier, but each attempt that reaches it has already cost a user lookup and, for a real account, a password verification; edge filtering sees only addresses yet drops a spread run before any hashing, so the two are complementary rather than alternatives.

[w2] Failed sign-ins land only in product telemetry today; a stuffing incident and the response to it (forced sign-outs, throttled accounts) is security history, which the catalog keeps in a separate audit record with its own audience and retention.
keyPoints.quote: Separates business telemetry from compliance history.

keyPoints.text: [w2] Caller-level detail goes into structured request logs keyed by request id, where support can answer one partner's question; metrics stay aggregated by bucket and route, which keeps them cheap and charts readable.
keyPoints.quote: Attach request ID, log on response finish as structured JSON.

keyPoints.text: [w1] Granting an allowance is a privileged action: put it behind a route-level permission and an audit record rather than an ad-hoc configuration change, so the question of who raised the partner's budget always has an answer.
keyPoints.quote: Rejects unauthorized access before business logic runs.
